title: Surface Cracks on the Tail-End Shaft Keyway
canonical_question: During a tail-shaft survey in dry dock, surface cracks are found on the keyway of the tail-end shaft. State the steps you would take as Chief Engineer to deal with the problem, and explain the effects if cracks of this kind are not dealt with at the proper time.

limb_of.limb_label: B. Surface cracks on the keyway of the tail-end shaft

sibling_limbs.limb_label: Surface crack on a propeller blade found in dry dock
sibling_limbs.owner_label: answered by the solved paper QP2603 Q7

present_day_examinable_core: Given a crack at the single most fatigue-prone location on the shafting, produce the Chief Engineer's sequence - contain, establish, notify, repair under class, prevent - and then explain the failure mode that makes the timing matter. The keyway limb is NOT the propeller-blade limb: a blade is a replaceable casting and the tail-end shaft is not, so the consequence of delay here is loss of propulsion and loss of watertight integrity rather than loss of efficiency.

recommended_exam_depth.note: MIW's recommendation for the second limb of a two-limb question. The sittings that evidence this family print a paper total only, with no per-question or per-limb split, so no mark here is inherited from any examiner's paper.

understand_first: A keyed propeller is not held on by its key. It is held by the interference grip of the taper, and the key is a safeguard that stops the propeller turning on the cone if that grip is ever lost. Candidates who believe the key transmits the torque write the wrong answer to this question, because they then treat a cracked keyway as a torque problem. It is a stress-concentration problem. The keyway is a square-cornered slot cut into the most highly stressed part of the shaft - the forward end of the taper, where the bending stress reverses once per revolution and where sea water can reach the steel past a worn aft seal. Sharp corners, a reversing stress field and an electrolyte is the classic recipe for corrosion fatigue, which is why the class rules single out this exact location for crack detection, and why a crack found here is a serious defect rather than a blemish.

blocks.h: Answer in two halves, because the question is in two halves

blocks.p: The examiner asks for steps and then for the effects of delay. Give them separately and label them. A single narrative that mixes actions with consequences loses the second half of the marks, because the consequences never get stated as consequences.

ul: Steps - contain and record; establish the extent by NDT; notify Company, Class and underwriters; agree a repair route with the attending surveyor; re-examine and re-certify; find the root cause and close it out.

Effects of delay - state the mechanism first (crack growth under reversed bending, accelerated by corrosion fatigue), then the physical outcome (shaft fracture, propeller loss, an open stern tube), then the statutory and commercial outcome (class withdrawn, casualty report, off-hire, and an insurance argument about known damage).
Name the location precisely. 'Forward end of the taper, at the keyway corner' earns more than 'on the shaft', because it shows you know why that is where it cracks.
Do not offer to weld it. Welding a tail-end shaft is not a repair a Chief Engineer proposes. Say instead what the class-approved routes are.

blocks.h: 1. Fix the situation before fixing the shaft

blocks.p: The shaft is out of service in a dock and the propeller is off, so there is no operational emergency. What there is instead is an evidence and authority problem: a defect affecting classification has been found, and everything that follows depends on it being recorded properly and reported to the right people before anybody starts grinding.

ul: Stop work on the shafting and prevent any further dressing, cleaning or handling of the cracked area. A crack that has been ground before it was measured cannot be measured.

Record it as found - photographs with a scale in frame, the position relative to the big end of the taper and to each end of the keyway, the orientation of the crack relative to the shaft axis, and the condition of the surrounding surface (corrosion pitting, fretting marks, evidence of a working key).
Raise it in the safety management system as a non-conformity or hazardous occurrence and inform the Designated Person Ashore, so that the report exists in the SMS and not only in a dock diary.

Preserve the surrounding evidence - aft seal and liner condition, stern tube oil analysis history, bearing wear-down readings, the propeller bore and key fit, and the shaft's own alignment records. Every one of these is an input to root cause, and every one of them disappears once the job is reassembled.

blocks.h: 2. Establish the nature and extent - this is a measurement job

blocks.p: A visible surface crack is a symptom. What matters to the repair decision is how deep it goes, how far it runs, and whether it is one crack or a family of them.

ul: Clean and examine by an approved surface crack detection method - magnetic particle inspection on the steel shaft, or dye penetrant where magnetisation is impractical - over the whole forward portion of the taper including the keyway and both its ends, not merely the visible defect. The class rules require crack detection over that region precisely because a single crack there is rarely alone.
Determine depth. Ultrasonic examination, and progressive local grinding with re-examination at each stage, establish whether this is a shallow surface indication or a developed fatigue crack.

Examine the matching features - the propeller keyway and bore, the key itself for signs of having carried load, and the taper contact area by blue bedding. A contact area short of the rule minimum tells you the grip was never right.

Have the examination witnessed by the attending classification surveyor and by the underwriters' surveyor, and get the NDT operator's certification and report into the file. An unwitnessed measurement will be argued about later.
Check the shaft against its rule diameter. How much metal may lawfully be removed is set by the shaft's designed scantling, and that number governs every repair option below.

blocks.h: 3. Notify - three separate audiences, three different reasons

rows: SMS reporting duty, and the commercial decision is theirs
Repair scope, budget, dock extension, and whether to charter in cover
A defect affecting class must be reported, and the shafting is a classed item whose survey is due here anyway
Whether the repair is acceptable, by whom it may be carried out, and whether a condition of class or a recommendation is imposed
Notice preserves the claim, and their surveyor's attendance at the examination is what makes cause arguable later
Whether the damage is an insured peril, wear and tear, or a latent defect, and what they will fund
Where the defect engages seaworthiness, or where the flag's own reporting rules require it
Whether a statutory report or an investigation follows

blocks.p: Notice to underwriters is early and factual. A Chief Engineer's report should describe what was found and measured and should not offer a conclusion about cause, because the cause is exactly what the policy turns on.

blocks.h: 4. Agree the repair route with the surveyor

blocks.p: The routes below are in the order they are normally considered. Which one applies is decided by depth, by how much metal the rule diameter allows to be lost, and by the surveyor - not by the Chief Engineer alone.

ol: Local removal and blending. The crack is ground out completely and the excavation blended into a generous radius, with the keyway corners radiused rather than left square, and the area re-examined by NDT to prove the crack has gone. This is the usual outcome for a shallow indication, and it also improves the detail that caused it.

Machining the taper. Where cracking and corrosion are spread over the cone, the taper may be re-machined to a fair surface. This moves the propeller forward on the cone, so the axial position must be recovered - typically by a spacer or distance piece at the coupling - and the bore must be re-bedded and the contact area re-proved.

Convert to a keyless fit, where depth or repeated cracking makes the keyway itself the problem. Removing the keyway removes the stress raiser altogether, and an oil-injection or press fit then transmits the torque entirely by friction. This is a design change: it needs class approval and the maker's calculation, and it is the permanent answer to a recurring keyway crack.

Renew the shaft. Where the crack is deep, where grinding it out would take the diameter below the rule scantling, or where the crack runs circumferentially rather than axially, the shaft is replaced, in class-approved certified material.

Welding is not a routine option. A tail-end shaft is a highly stressed forging and welding on it is not permitted as a general repair. Any proposal of that kind belongs to the society and the shaft maker, not to the ship.

blocks.p: Close the job properly. Re-assemble to the maker's procedure - pull-up or oil-injection figures recorded, contact area proved, key fit checked, aft seal renewed, stern tube oil renewed and sampled - and record the final NDT clearance. Where the society is not fully satisfied it will impose a condition of class with a date; that date is then a maintenance commitment, and letting it lapse suspends class as surely as the original crack would have.

blocks.h: 5. Root cause, because the crack is a message

blocks.p: A keyway crack is a fatigue crack, and fatigue cracks come from a stress the shaft was not designed to see, from a detail that concentrates the stress it was, or from an environment that helps the crack along. Each of those has a different fix.

ul: Loss of taper grip. If the interference fit was never right, or was lost through corrosion or incorrect pull-up, the propeller works on the cone and drives the key - which puts a torque load into a slot that was never meant to carry one. Evidence: fretting in the bore, a bright or hammered key, contact area below the rule minimum.

Sea water at the steel. A worn or leaking aft seal admits sea water into the taper and keyway. With a reversing stress field this becomes corrosion fatigue, in which a crack grows at a stress well below the dry fatigue limit. Evidence: pitting, rust staining out of the keyway, water in the stern tube oil.

The detail itself. Sharp keyway corners, a badly cut keyway, or a keyway ending too close to the big end of the cone. Fix it in the repair - radius the corners rather than simply restoring the geometry that failed.

Abnormal loading. Prolonged running in or near the barred speed range, a torsional resonance, heavy propeller-induced vibration, a damaged or fouled propeller running out of balance, ice contact or a grounding, or severe misalignment and bearing wear-down putting bending into the cone.

Fix the cause in the plan, not in the report. Whatever is found should come back as a change to the maintenance system - seal renewal interval, stern tube oil sampling, wear-down recording, barred-speed discipline, propeller inspection each dock - and it should be verified at the next internal audit.

blocks.h: 6. The effects if the cracks are not dealt with at the proper time

blocks.p: This is the half of the question most answers under-write. Give the mechanism first, then the outcomes.

ul: The crack grows, and it grows fastest here. Every revolution reverses the bending stress at the forward end of the taper. A crack at a square keyway corner is a ready-made initiation site, and once started it propagates under a load the intact shaft carried comfortably. Sea water accelerates it. Growth is not linear: it is slow, and then it is sudden.
Fatigue failure of the tail-end shaft, typically at or just forward of the taper - and there is no warning stage a watchkeeper can act on.

Loss of the propeller and the after length of shaft. Total and immediate loss of propulsion, leaving a drifting vessel - dangerous anywhere, and far worse in a traffic separation scheme, in restricted water, or on a lee shore.

Loss of watertight integrity. Once the shaft leaves the stern tube, the tube is an open hole below the waterline. Progressive flooding of the after spaces, loss of stability margin, and in the worst case loss of the ship - which is what makes this a safety question rather than a maintenance question.
Secondary damage. A shaft failing under load can wreck the stern tube bearings and seals, damage the after peak structure, and overspeed the main engine at the instant the load disappears.

Statutory and class consequences. Class suspended or withdrawn; the certificates founded on class fall with it; a casualty report and investigation follow; and flag State and port State will both want the survey history.

Commercial and insurance consequences. Emergency dry docking and towage, a far larger repair than the one avoided, off-hire and cargo claims - and an argument with underwriters that the owner is likely to lose, because a defect that was found, recorded and then left is known damage and the duty to maintain the ship's condition after survey was not discharged. A crack that could have been ground out in a scheduled dock becomes an uninsured casualty.

blocks.p: The one-sentence answer to the second half. A cracked propeller blade costs efficiency and, at worst, a blade. A cracked tail-end shaft keyway costs the propeller, the propulsion and potentially the ship - which is why the two limbs of this question are not the same question.

The marks in this limb sit in three places: the authority sequence (Company, Class, underwriters - and knowing what each of them decides), the named repair routes together with the constraint that governs them (the rule diameter), and the mechanism of delay. Weak answers describe a repair in loving mechanical detail and never mention the classification society, which is the one party that decides whether the repair is acceptable at all.

ul: Treating the key as the torque path. It is not, and the whole diagnosis changes if you think it is. The taper grip transmits the torque; the key is a safeguard. A working key is evidence of a defective fit.

Answering the propeller-blade limb twice. The blade limb and the keyway limb share an opening scenario and nothing else. If your answer would be equally true of a cracked blade, you have not answered this limb.

blocks.h: What this answer deliberately does not claim

blocks.p: It gives no permissible crack depth, no grinding limit, no minimum taper contact percentage, no pull-up figure and no survey interval. Those are set by the individual society's rules and the shaft maker's data for the specific shaft, and they differ between societies and by seal and lubrication arrangement. A universal figure would be worse than none, because it would be quoted in an exam as though it were a rule. What the answer does state is the correct source for each of them.

blocks.h: How this sits beside the solved paper

blocks.p: The first limb of this family - the surface crack found on a propeller blade - is answered by MIW's solved QP2603 Q7, and that answer was reused rather than rewritten. This entry exists only because no solved MIW paper sets the tail-end shaft keyway.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Stop, record and report before you grind. NDT the whole forward taper including the keyway, establish depth, and have Class and the H&M surveyor witness it. Then the routes in order: grind out and radius; re-machine the taper with a spacer; convert to keyless; renew the shaft. Never weld it. Root cause is lost taper grip, sea water past the aft seal, a sharp keyway corner, or abnormal torsional loading. Leave it and the crack grows by corrosion fatigue to a shaft fracture - propeller gone, propulsion gone, stern tube open to the sea, class withdrawn, and the claim lost as known damage.
critical_numbers: None quoted, on purpose. Permissible crack depth, grinding limits, minimum taper contact area and pull-up figures are set by the individual classification society's rules and by the shaft maker's data for that shaft, and they differ between societies - see the study guide.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: IACS Unified Requirement Z21 and the individual society's rules govern the screwshaft survey and require crack detection by an approved method in way of the forward portion of the taper INCLUDING the keyway, with the propeller drawn where the shaft is keyed. SOLAS chapter I regulation 11 requires the condition of the ship to be maintained after survey and requires damage or defect to be reported. The ISM Code makes it a non-conformity to be reported to the DPA. Nothing in SOLAS prescribes the repair - that is class and the shaft maker.
quick_revision.major_trap: Writing the propeller-blade answer again, or proposing to weld the tail-end shaft. The second is worse: it is the one answer that tells the examiner you do not know what kind of component you are dealing with.

authority_sources.source: IACS Unified Requirement Z21 and IACS member society rules - survey of screwshafts and tube shafts, including crack detection by an approved method in way of the forward portion of the taper and the keyway, with the propeller drawn where the shaft is keyed
authority_sources.checked: Stated at the level on which the unified requirement and the member societies agree: that the forward part of the taper INCLUDING the keyway is a designated crack-detection area at the shaft survey, and that a keyed propeller must be drawn for it. MIW has NOT read UR Z21 at source for this entry, and quotes from it no survey interval, no permissible depth and no grinding limit, because the survey types, intervals and acceptance limits differ between societies and by lubrication and seal arrangement. That variation is declared here rather than averaged into a single figure.

authority_sources.source: SOLAS chapter I regulation 11 - maintenance of conditions after survey, and the duty to report damage or defect affecting the condition of the ship
authority_sources.checked: Read at source and confirmed in force and unamended in substance as at 24 August 2026. Cited only for the two propositions it actually supports - that the condition of the ship must be maintained after survey, and that damage or a defect must be reported so that an investigation and any necessary survey follow. It prescribes no repair method and this answer does not suggest that it does.

authority_sources.source: ISM Code - reporting and analysis of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences, and the role of the Designated Person Ashore
authority_sources.checked: Read at source and confirmed in force as at 24 August 2026. Cited for the reporting duty and the DPA link, which is what turns a dock-floor finding into a governed record.

authority_sources.source: Fatigue and corrosion-fatigue behaviour of a keyed propeller shaft taper - stress concentration at the square keyway corner, reversal of bending stress once per revolution at the forward end of the cone, and crack growth below the dry fatigue limit in the presence of sea water; torque transmitted by the interference grip of the taper with the key as a safeguard
authority_sources.checked: Settled engineering with no governing instrument, declared as such. The mechanism is framework-independent and unchanged, and it is also the reason the class rules single out this location, so the engineering and the survey requirement corroborate each other rather than either standing alone.

review_record.reviewer: Laptop Claude Code (independent clean-context review pass)
review_record.notes: Reviewed against the question, the cited authority and nothing else. FOUR things were checked, and two of them are the reason to trust this entry rather than merely accept it. SCOPE first, because this is a limb entry and the characteristic failure of a limb entry is answering its sibling. It does not: the propeller blade appears once, in the closing sentence, and only to draw the distinction that the two limbs carry different consequences. Nothing in the body would be true of a cracked blade. SECOND, the numbers - and the finding is that there are none, deliberately. The entry declines to give a permissible crack depth, a grinding limit, a contact-area percentage or a survey interval, and says in terms why: those figures differ between societies and by shaft arrangement. That is the correct treatment, and it is the same treatment CA-EM-0001 gave the lay-up survey interval, so the library is consistent with itself. A reviewer looking for a wrong number found no number to be wrong. THIRD, the authority split is honestly drawn. SOLAS I/11 is cited for maintenance of condition and for reporting, and expressly NOT for a repair method; the survey requirement is labelled CLASSIFICATION_SOCIETY_SUMMARY with an express statement that UR Z21 was not read at source; the fatigue mechanism is labelled ENGINEERING_JUDGEMENT. No claim is dressed in a stronger class than it earns. FOURTH, exam utility. The second half of the printed task - the effects of not dealing with the cracks at the proper time - is answered as a mechanism followed by consequences, and it reaches the two facts that make this a safety answer: loss of propulsion, and an open stern tube. The entry also refuses the one technically wrong thing a candidate might otherwise write, that the shaft could be welded. PASS.

next_review_trigger: Re-review if (a) IACS materially revises UR Z21 or a member society changes its screwshaft survey or crack-detection requirements, (b) SOLAS chapter I regulation 11 is amended, or (c) MIW solves a past paper that sets the tail-end shaft or its keyway directly, in which case the relationship between that sitting-anchored answer and this one must be adjudicated rather than assumed. Routine re-review at twenty-four months rather than twelve: the mechanism is engineering and does not move, and the class detail moves slowly.
